stem: A uniform footbridge plank AB of length $3.0\ \text{m}$ and weight $600\ \text{N}$ is hinged to a river bank at A and held horizontal by a cable from B to the top of a post above A. The cable makes $50^\circ$ with the plank. A man of weight $400\ \text{N}$ stands $2.4\ \text{m}$ from A.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: State the two conditions for the plank to be in equilibrium.

points.description: The resultant force on it is zero.
The resultant torque (moment) about any point is zero.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: There is no resultant force on the plank, and there is no resultant moment about any point.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: By taking moments about A, calculate the tension in the cable, in N, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the components of the force exerted by the hinge on the plank, in N, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: horizontal component

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: vertical component (upwards positive)

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: The man walks slowly from A towards B. Explain how the tension in the cable changes.

points.description: His moment about A increases as his distance from A increases.
The cable's moment about A must increase to balance it, and its perpendicular distance from A is fixed, so the tension increases (linearly with his distance).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: As he moves away from A his weight has a larger moment about A. The cable's moment must increase to balance it; its perpendicular distance from A does not change, so the tension increases steadily.

explanation: Moments about the hinge give the tension; resolving gives the hinge force.
hints: Take moments about A to eliminate the hinge force.
Perpendicular distance of the cable from A = 3.0 sin 50°.

stem: A navigation buoy is a closed vertical cylinder of radius $0.30\ \text{m}$, height $1.20\ \text{m}$ and mass $140\ \text{kg}$. It floats upright in sea water of density $1025\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$. Atmospheric pressure is $1.01 \times 10^{5}\ \text{Pa}$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain, in terms of pressure, the origin of the upthrust on the buoy.

points.description: Pressure in a fluid increases with depth (p = ρgh).
The pressure on the bottom face is greater than on the top, so there is a resultant upward force.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Pressure in the water increases with depth, so the water pushes up on the bottom of the buoy harder than it (or the air) pushes down on the top: the resultant upward force is the upthrust.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the depth to which the buoy floats, in m, to three significant figures.
parts.explanation: Upthrust = weight: $\rho g (\pi r^2 d) = mg$, so $d = \dfrac{140}{1025 \times \pi \times 0.30^2} = 0.483\ \text{m}$.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Upthrust = weight: $\rho g (\pi r^2 d) = mg$, so $d = \dfrac{140}{1025 \times \pi \times 0.30^2} = 0.483\ \text{m}$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the total pressure on the bottom of the buoy, in Pa, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the largest extra mass of equipment that can be fixed to the top of the buoy before it sinks, in kg, to three significant figures.
parts.explanation: Fully submerged it displaces $\pi r^2 H$; extra mass $= \rho\pi r^2 (H - d) = 208\ \text{kg}$.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Fully submerged it displaces $\pi r^2 H$; extra mass $= \rho\pi r^2 (H - d) = 208\ \text{kg}$.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: The buoy drifts from the sea into a fresh-water estuary. State and explain what happens to the depth at which it floats.

points.description: It floats deeper (lower).
Fresh water is less dense, so a larger volume must be displaced to give an upthrust equal to the (unchanged) weight.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: It floats lower in the water: the weight is unchanged, but fresh water is less dense, so a larger volume must be displaced to produce the same upthrust.

explanation: Floating: upthrust = weight; the pressure at depth is p₀ + ρgh.

stem: A haulage truck of total mass $3.6 \times 10^{4}\ \text{kg}$ climbs a long straight hill at a constant speed of $15\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. The road rises $4.0\ \text{m}$ for every $100\ \text{m}$ travelled along it. The total resistive force on the truck is $5200\ \text{N}$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Define power.

points.description: Work done (or energy transferred) per unit time.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Power is the work done per unit time.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Show that the power developed by a force F moving its point of application at a constant velocity v in the direction of the force is Fv.

points.description: P = W/t and W = F × s (displacement in the direction of the force).
P = F s/t = Fv since s/t = v.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Power = work done ÷ time = (F × s)/t; since s/t is the velocity v, P = Fv.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the driving force on the truck, in N, to three significant figures.
parts.explanation: Weight component down the slope $= mg\sin\theta = 3.6 \times 10^{4} \times 9.81 \times 0.040 = 14130\ \text{N}$. Driving force $= 5200 + 14130 = 19300\ \text{N}$.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Weight component down the slope $= mg\sin\theta = 3.6 \times 10^{4} \times 9.81 \times 0.040 = 14130\ \text{N}$. Driving force $= 5200 + 14130 = 19300\ \text{N}$.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the useful power output of the engine, in W, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: The engine is 38% efficient. Calculate the rate at which energy is supplied by the fuel, in W, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: At the top of the hill the road becomes level and the engine keeps the same power output. Explain what happens to the speed of the truck.

points.description: The weight component is no longer opposing motion, so the driving force P/v exceeds the resistive force and the truck accelerates.
As speed rises, P/v falls and resistance rises until they are equal: the truck reaches a new, higher constant speed.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: On the level the slope component disappears, so the driving force P/v is larger than the resistive force and the truck accelerates. As it speeds up the driving force falls and the resistance rises until they balance at a new, higher steady speed.

explanation: Driving force = resistance + mg sin θ; power = Fv; input = output ÷ efficiency.
hints: Find the component of weight along the slope.
P = Fv with the driving force.

stem: A steel guy wire supporting a radio mast is $12.0\ \text{m}$ long and $4.0\ \text{mm}$ in diameter. Its tension is $2.5 \times 10^{3}\ \text{N}$. The Young modulus of the steel is $2.0 \times 10^{11}\ \text{Pa}$, and the wire obeys Hooke's law.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Define tensile stress and tensile strain.

points.description: Tensile stress: (tensile) force per unit cross-sectional area.
Tensile strain: extension per unit original length.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Tensile stress is the tensile force per unit cross-sectional area; tensile strain is the extension per unit original length.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the stress in the wire, in Pa, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the extension of the wire, in m, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the elastic potential energy stored in the wire, in J, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: During a storm the tension rises so much that the wire is stretched beyond its elastic limit. Describe and explain what is observed when the storm passes.

points.description: The wire does not return to its original length: it has a permanent extension (it sags/becomes slack).
Beyond the elastic limit, layers of atoms slip (plastic deformation), and these do not move back when the load is reduced.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: When the tension falls the wire keeps a permanent extension, so it is slacker than before. Beyond the elastic limit layers of atoms slid past one another and these new positions remain when the load is removed.

explanation: σ = F/A, ε = σ/E, x = εL and Ep = ½Fx within the limit of proportionality.
hints: Area = πd²/4 with d in metres.

stem: A car of mass $1100\ \text{kg}$ travels at a constant speed of $13\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ round a flat, horizontal bend that is an arc of a circle of radius $45\ \text{m}$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain why the car is accelerating even though its speed is constant.

points.description: Velocity is a vector; its direction is changing continuously.
So the velocity changes, which is an acceleration (directed towards the centre of the bend).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Velocity is a vector and the direction of the car's motion keeps changing, so its velocity changes: it has an acceleration, towards the centre of the bend.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the angular speed of the car about the centre of the bend, in $\text{rad s}^{-1}$, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the centripetal force on the car, in N, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: The maximum sideways friction is $0.62$ times the car's weight. Calculate the greatest speed at which it can take the bend, in $\text{m s}^{-1}$, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Later the car crosses the top of a hump of radius $30\ \text{m}$ at $12\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Calculate the normal contact force of the road on the car at the top, in N, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Explain why the passengers feel lighter at the top of the hump.

points.description: The normal (contact) force on them is less than their weight, because part of their weight provides the centripetal force.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The seat pushes up on them with less than their weight, because part of their weight is used to provide the centripetal force towards the centre below.

explanation: Friction provides mv²/r on the flat bend; at the top of a hump, mg − N = mv²/r.
hints: Which real force points to the centre on the flat bend?
At the top of the hump the centre is below the car.

stem: On a fairground ride, each seat hangs from a chain $6.0\ \text{m}$ long attached to the edge of a rotating roof. Treat each seat and rider (total mass $60\ \text{kg}$) as a conical pendulum whose chain is attached to a fixed point on the axis; it makes one revolution every $4.2\ \text{s}$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Define the radian.

points.description: The angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the angular speed, in $\text{rad s}^{-1}$, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Show that the tension in the chain is $T = mL\omega^2$, where $L$ is the chain length.

points.description: Horizontally: $T\sin\theta = mr\omega^2$, where $r = L\sin\theta$ is the radius of the circle.
So $T\sin\theta = mL\sin\theta\,\omega^2$ and $T = mL\omega^2$.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The horizontal component of tension provides the centripetal force: $T\sin\theta = mr\omega^2$ with $r = L\sin\theta$. Cancelling $\sin\theta$ gives $T = mL\omega^2$.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the tension in the chain, in N, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Calculate the angle between the chain and the vertical, in degrees, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Calculate the speed of the rider, in m/s, to three significant figures.
parts.explanation: $r = L\sin\theta = 4.10\ \text{m}$; $v = r\omega = 6.13\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Using $L$ as the radius overestimates it.
parts.workedSolution: 1. $r = L\sin\theta = 4.10\ \text{m}$; $v = r\omega = 6.13\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Using $L$ as the radius overestimates it.

explanation: Horizontal component of tension = mrω² with r = L sin θ, giving T = mLω²; the vertical component balances the weight.
hints: The radius of the circle is L sin θ, not L.
Resolve the tension vertically to find θ.
